transcript.text:
Greyhollow clings to the shoulder of a mountain like a bird's nest in a gale, its houses cut back into the stone to keep out of the wind. It is a town that lives by what it digs from under the earth, and the whole of it answers to the Anvil Father: forger of stone, god of honest toil, whose hammer rings in every seam of ore a dwarf has ever prized. For six years Brakka Ironvein stood guard at the Father's temple, and he knows the town's sounds as well as his own heartbeat — the clang of the stamps, the creak of the headframes, the low rumour of men coming up from a shift with their lamps guttering.

Three days ago, three miners went down into the old north workings, the ones sealed a generation back and left to the dark. None of them came up. Last night a fourth man did — alone, his lamp dead in his hand, his eyes fixed on something no one else could see. He spoke of lights that walked, and then he died before dawn. Now the town council means to brick that entrance over at sunrise tomorrow, missing miners or not. And Hessa, the temple's old prior, has asked Brakka to go down before then, and bring back whoever can still be brought back.

It is late afternoon. Brakka stands at the mine mouth, the borrowed temple lantern in his hand, the cold leaking out of the dark beyond the half-pulled timbers. Behind him, Greyhollow is going about its evening; ahead, the old workings wait.

What does Brakka do?

I check the ground at the mine mouth for tracks or drag marks before stepping in, then tie off a length of rope to the nearest sound timber so I can find my way back. Once that's done, I raise the lantern and head in slowly, keeping my shield up.

An ability check tests a character's or monster's innate talent and training in an effort to overcome a challenge. Each ability covers a broad range of capabilities, including skills that a character or a monster can be proficient in. A skill represents a specific aspect of an ability score, and an individual's proficiency in a skill demonstrates a focus on that aspect. (A character's starting skill proficiencies are determined at character creation, and a monster's skill proficiencies appear in the monster's stat block.)

For example, a Dexterity check might reflect a character's attempt to pull off an acrobatic stunt, to palm an object, or to stay hidden. Each of these aspects of Dexterity has an associated skill: Acrobatics, Sleight of Hand, and Stealth, respectively. So a character who has proficiency in the Stealth skill is particularly good at Dexterity checks related to sneaking and hiding.

Sometimes, the GM might ask for an ability check using a specific skill-for example, "Make a Wisdom (Perception) check." At other times, a player might ask the GM if proficiency in a particular skill applies to a check. In either case, proficiency in a skill means an individual can add his or her proficiency bonus to ability checks that involve that skill. Without proficiency in the skill, the individual makes a normal ability check.

For example, if a character attempts to climb up a dangerous cliff, the GM might ask for a Strength (Athletics) check. If the character is proficient in Athletics, the character's proficiency bonus is added to the Strength check. If the character lacks that proficiency, he or she just makes a Strength check.

#### Variant: Skills with Different Abilities

Normally, your proficiency in a skill applies only to a specific kind of ability check. Proficiency in Athletics, for example, usually applies to Strength checks. In some situations, though, your proficiency might reasonably apply to a different kind of check. In such cases, the GM might ask for a check using an unusual combination of ability and skill, or you might ask your GM if you can apply a proficiency to a different check. For example, if you have to swim from an offshore island to the mainland, your GM might call for a Constitution check to see if you have the stamina to make it that far. In this case, your GM might allow you to apply your proficiency in Athletics and ask for a Constitution (Athletics) check. So if you're proficient in Athletics, you apply your proficiency bonus to the Constitution check just as you would normally do for a Strength (Athletics) check. Similarly, when your half-orc barbarian uses a display of raw strength to intimidate an enemy, your GM might ask for a Strength (Intimidation) check, even though Intimidation is normally associated with Charisma.

Brakka kneels at the mine mouth and lets his eyes run over the churned ground before the timbers. It is not hard reading. Three sets of boot-prints lead inward, their edges softened by three days of settling — the missing miners, going down together. Over them and around them, one lone set comes back out, scuffed and uneven, as though the fourth man had dragged himself up on hands and knees. The trampling of the men who carried him home lies on top of all of it, but Brakka can still make out the older marks underneath. No drag-marks lead inward; nobody was pulled down against their will. The three walked in on their own feet.

He ties one end of the hempen rope to a sound timber at the mouth, takes a turn round his fist to pay it out as he goes, and raises the borrowed lantern. The light reaches thirty paces ahead and no further; beyond that the dark is absolute. Shield up, he steps through the gap and into the old workings.

The air changes at once. It is colder by a breath, and wet, and it carries a smell Brakka knows from every mine he has ever stood in: stone dust and old wood and water seeping somewhere out of sight. The drift runs gently downward, timbered with oak so dark it looks black, the floor worn smooth by long-dead boots. Dust lies thick beyond the trampled patch at the entrance, disturbed only by the three sets of inward boots and the one scuffed set leading back out, and it drinks the lamplight. Somewhere far off, water drips, slow and even, like a pulse.

What does Brakka do?
I follow the three sets of boot-prints down the drift, paying out rope as I go and stopping every twenty paces or so to listen. I keep an eye on the timbers overhead for any sign of weakness.

Brakka follows the boot-prints down the drift, the rope whispering through his fist. The floor keeps its gentle downward lean, and the timbers grow older as he goes — black with damp, some of them split along the grain, though nothing looks ready to give way under his weight. He reads the wood as a miner reads it: sound enough, for now, but he steps where the floor is worn and the supports are plumb.

At the twentieth pace or so the rope runs out. All fifty feet of it, paid out and trailing back through the dark to the timber at the mouth, and it goes taut in his hand like a fish on a line. The drift still runs down and away ahead of him, and the three sets of prints go on into the black, unbothered. Fifty feet is all the thread he has to find his way back.

He stops to listen, as he has done at each halt, and this time the mine answers.

It is very faint, at the very edge of hearing: a dragging sound, slow and rhythmic, like a foot that is not properly lifted, or a body being pulled along stone. It comes and goes, and it comes from somewhere far down the drift, beyond the lantern's reach. And in the same moment — so brief he is not sure he saw it at all — a pale light glimmers in the deep dark, drifts sideways, and is gone. Not the warm yellow of a lamp or the red of a torch. A cold, grey-green glimmer, low to the floor, walking.

What does Brakka do?

I stay put, shutter the lantern down to a thin slit, and slip back a few steps to the edge of the rope's reach so I'm not standing in a pool of light. Then I wait a moment, shield braced, to see whether that dragging sound or the grey-green glow comes closer.

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

## The story so far (turns 1–10)

**World and setup.** Greyhollow is a dwarf mining town cut into a cold mountainside. Its god is the Anvil Father (forge, stone, honest toil). Brakka Ironvein, a hill dwarf fighter and acolyte of the Anvil Father, served six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father there.

Three days ago (9th of Leaffall, 1214) three miners — **Orrin** (young dwarf, quiet, not long out of apprenticeship), **Davor**, and **Osrik** (older, broad-shouldered, deep-seam man with a loud laugh) — went down into the old north workings, sealed a generation ago (~30 years). None came back. Last night (11th) a fourth man came up alone babbling about "lights that walk" and died before dawn. The town council will brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow (13th). Hessa, the temple's old dwarf prior, asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back. The session opened late afternoon (Day 1, 12th Leaffall, ~4:30 PM) at the mine mouth with a borrowed hooded lantern.

**What happened.** Brakka read the ground at the mouth (Survival 15): three boot-prints leading in, one scuffed set coming out (the fourth man crawling), rescuers' trampling on top; no drag-marks inward — the three walked in freely. He tied his 50 ft of rope to a timber and descended, following the prints, stopping to listen. The rope ran out after about twenty paces; he began cutting crosses into timbers as waymarks instead. On a listen (Perception 18) he heard a dragging sound and glimpsed a cold grey-green light low to the floor.

He shuttered the lantern and hid; a Stealth check came up natural 1, and the thing noticed him. It was one of the missing miners reanimated — a zombie — shambling with a dragging leg and a lamp burning cold grey-green light that gave hardly any glow. In the fight that followed Brakka was hit once (7 damage, to 7/14), used **Second Wind** (healed 3, to 10/14; now spent), and killed it with a **natural 20** critical that decapitated it (the crit bypassed Undead Fortitude). +50 XP (now 50/300). He recognised the dead man as **Orrin**.

He closed the severed head's eyes and prayed over him. Examining the body (Medicine 14): the killing wound was three long parallel claw-tears across the chest, bloodless; the fingertips were raw and nail-split from clawing at stone in the dark. Orrin died slowly, clawing at the walls, and something came for him. He wore an iron hammer charm of the Anvil Father on a cord, which Brakka left on the body. Brakka took Orrin's miner's pick and the now-dead cold green lamp, drew Orrin's cloak over his face, and went deeper.

He followed the two remaining sets of prints to a low stope containing the miners' camp: a cold fire, two packs (tagged **Davor** and **Osrik**), and a single right boot with snapped laces, dropped in flight. Davor's pack held a charcoal map of the old workings marking a route to an **X labelled "pocket"** deep down; Osrik's pack held rations, lamp oil, cord, a matching iron hammer charm, and a half-eaten loaf. Brakka took the map and Osrik's charm (to carry back to his family).

**Where things stand at the end of turn 10.** Brakka is in the old north workings, at the stope camp, HP 10/14, Second Wind spent, XP 50/300. He carries the borrowed hooded lantern (lit), plus: miner's pick, the dead cold-green lamp, the charcoal map, and Osrik's hammer charm. The two remaining miners (Davor and Osrik) are somewhere deeper; a narrow passage leads down from the stope toward the map's X.

**Hidden decisions not yet revealed in play.** The "lights that walk" are not carried lamps — they are living cold grey-green flames with a will of their own (will-o'-wisp-like), that hover near and accompany the reanimated dead. The reanimated miners are zombies (SRD Zombie stat block, Undead Fortitude, slam +3/1d6+1, AC 8, HP 22, speed 20 ft, passive perception 8). The miners were seeking a rumoured rich ore "pocket" marked on Davor's map; the mine was sealed ~30 years ago to contain something (the exact deep cause — a malevolent undead presence that raises the dead and is served by the wisps — is still to be determined, but the wisps feed on the despair of the lost/dying; keep it consistent that the light is a separate living thing from the corpse). Osrik is now one of the reanimated dead; Davor is deeper (the second fainter light). The fourth man is dead in town.
